bio.en: Uri Levine is co-founder of Waze and nine other companies, has sold two companies for over $1 billion, advised 50+ founders, and authored Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution.
bio.zh: Uri Levine 是 Waze 与另外九家公司的联合创始人，曾将两家公司以超 10 亿美元售出，为 50 多位创始人提供过顾问服务，并著有《爱上问题，而非方案》（Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution）。

summary.en: Uri distills the biggest lessons from working with dozens of startups into one core idea: fall in love with the problem, not the solution. He shares why founders should validate the pain before building, stay ready to pivot when the data disagrees, and keep the user's problem front and center through every stage. The episode is a founder's field guide to building companies that actually matter.
summary.zh: Uri 将他与数十家初创公司共事所得的最大经验，提炼为一个核心理念：爱上问题，而非方案。他分享了为什么创始人应当在动手前先验证“痛点”、在数据相悖时随时准备转型，以及为何要在每个阶段都把用户的问题置于最前沿。本期是一份创始人的实战指南，关于打造真正有意义的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what's really interesting to me is that from all of that experience, the biggest startup lesson you seem to have taken out of that is to fall in love with the problem. It's what your book is called. You have a T-shirt that you're wearing right now that you wear on every podcast that says that exactly. Clearly this lesson has struck a big chord with you. turns.zh: 我觉得最让我感兴趣的是，在你所有创业经历中，你似乎从中领悟到的最重要的一课，就是要"爱上你所面临的问题"。这正是你书的书名所在。你现在穿的这件T恤，每次做播客时都会穿，上面就印着这句话。显然，这个道理对你触动很深。我很好奇，是否有某个瞬间让你意识到，这才是创业的核心所在，也是每个创业者必须掌握的关键。是否有某个顿悟的时刻，还是说这只是一种循序渐进的领悟过程——"哦，天哪，也许这就是成功的秘诀"？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I'm not sure that this is a certain moment. I think that that was evolving over time and realizing that, look, at the end of the day, the entrepreneurship journey is about value creation. The simplest way to create value is solve a problem. That's the simplest way. And in my background, I'm an engineer always looking for the simplest way, and solve a problem is the simplest way, and so this is where fall in love with the problem coming from, and people occasionally would confuse the T-shirt with the book, and now the T-shirt is about 10 or even more years old and the book is only two years old, and so I was wearing those T-shirts for a long while before I wrote the book and when I wrote the book that was obvious that this is going to be the name of the book, but they are way more into that, right? (00:04:06): So when you fall in love with the problem, then what happened is that the problem is going to serve as the North Star of your journey, and when you have a North Star, you're going to make less deviation from the course and you are way more likely to become successful. But also the story that you are about to tell is way more compelling. Just imagine that we will be here in 2007, just before I started Waze, and I will tell you I'm going to build an AI crowd-source based navigation system and you're going to say, "Oh, yeah, very interesting," but you don't care. If I will tell you I'm going to help you to avoid traffic jams, then you do care, and when your customer cares, they want you to be successful, and when they want you to be successful, they are going to help you to become successful. (00:04:56): And so in that sense, fall in love with the problem is really a key to increase the likelihood of being successful. So in general, all of my startups start with a problem. Think of a problem, a big problem, something that it's worth solving, something that the world will become a better place if you solve that and then ask yourself, so who has this problem? If you happen to be the only person on the planet with this problem, I can recommend you a therapist. Don't build a startup. It's way more expensive and takes way longer period of time to build a startup. But if a lot of people actually have this problem, what you really want to do next is go and speak with those people and understand their perception of the problem and only then start to build the solution. If you follow this path and your solution works, it's guaranteed that you're creating value. (00:05:47): If you start with a solution, you might be building something that no one cares and that's really frustrating. So fall in love with the problem. This is where you want to start. Now this is really hard because I am getting tons of emails every week from entrepreneurs and they all start with what we are doing and I don't really care what you're doing. What I really care about is why you are doing that, and this is the problem that you solve or the value that you create or the value that you create for me. This is what really matters, right? And so if you start your story with, "Our company is," or, "Our system is," and in the recent year everything is, "Our AI system is," or, "Our AI company is." But generally speaking, if you start your story with that, you focus on your solution. If you start with the story with, "The problem we are solving is," Then you focus on the problem. If your story start with, "The value that we create for you is," then you focus on the user. The last two are way better than focus on the solution.
turns.zh: 我不确定这是否是一个特定的时刻。我认为这是一个随着时间演变的过程，最终意识到，归根结底，创业之旅就是创造价值。最简单的创造价值方式就是解决问题。对于我而言，我是一名工程师，总是在寻找最简单的方法，而解决问题就是最简单的方法。因此，我深深爱上了源于问题的挑战。有些人偶尔会把我的T恤和我的书混淆起来。这件T恤已经有10多年历史了，而这本书才出版两年。在写书之前，我很长时间都穿着这件T恤。当我开始写书时，很明显这本书就应该以它命名，但人们更关注的是T恤本身，对吧？（00:04:06）：所以当你爱上问题时，问题就会成为你旅程的北极星。当你有了北极星，就能更少地偏离轨道，更容易成功。同时，你的故事也会更有感染力。想象一下，2007年我们刚创立Waze前夕，如果我告诉你我要开发一个基于AI和众包的导航系统，你可能会说：“哦，真有趣。”但你并不在意。但如果我说我要帮你避开交通堵塞，你就会感兴趣。当客户感兴趣时，他们就希望你成功，而当他们希望你成功时，他们就会助你一臂之力。（00:04:56）：从这个角度看，爱上问题确实是提高成功概率的关键。因此，我所有的创业项目都始于一个问题。想一个大问题，一个值得解决的问题，一个解决后世界会变得更美好的问题，然后问自己，谁会遇到这个问题？如果你是地球上唯一一个有这个问题的人，我建议你去看心理医生，而不是创业。创业成本高昂，耗时漫长。但如果很多人都有这个问题，你接下来要做的是去和这些人交流，理解他们对问题的看法，然后再着手开发解决方案。如果你遵循这个路径，解决方案一旦成功，就一定能创造价值。（00:05:47）：如果你从解决方案入手，就可能打造出无人问津的产品，这实在令人沮丧。所以要爱上问题。从这里出发。这很难，因为每周我都会收到大量创业者的邮件，他们都从“我们公司是”或者“我们的系统是”开头。但我真正关心的是你为什么要做这件事，你解决了什么问题，或者为我创造了什么价值。这才是关键，对吧？所以如果你以 “我们的公司是” 开头讲故事，或者近年来都以 “我们的AI系统是” 开头，但通常如果你以 “我们要解决的问题是” 开头讲故事，就会把焦点放在问题上。如果以 “我们为你创造的价值是” 开头讲故事，就会把焦点放在用户身上。后两种方式远比聚焦解决方案要好得多。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So people ask me, "So you send me to speak with users. How many?" And I will tell them a hundred. You don't need a hundred, but the hundred basically say you need to get out of your comfort zone. It's not just your close friends and family that you need to discuss that. You need to discuss that with people that you don't know. And usually what happen is, and the validation is in most cases is really clear, right? If you tell someone, "This is the problem I'm going to address," and they will tell you, "Oh, I know someone that has this problem," it's not a real problem. If they will tell you, "No, no, no, no, no. This is not the problem. The problem is," and they will give you their description of the problem. This is something that you really want to follow. So if you speak with a hundred people, but if you actually speak with 20 people that you don't know, you will get validated whether or not this problem is real or not. (00:10:23): And look, it's not the only way to become successful, right? You look at one of the most successful products in the world, the iPhone, right? And you ask yourself, what was exactly the problem when they started? And the answer is that there was no problem when they started. There were smartphones and people were actually very happy with them. And so occasionally we need to invent something completely new, but solving a problem is simply the simplest way to create value.
turns.zh:
有人问我：“你让我去和用户交流，有多少人啊？”我会告诉他们是一百人。你不需要一百个人，但这100个人基本上都在告诉你，你需要走出舒适区。不能只和亲朋好友讨论这些问题，你还需要和陌生人交流。通常情况下，验证结果往往非常清晰。例如，如果你告诉某人：“这是我要解决的问题。”对方会说：“哦，我认识有这个问题的人。”那就说明这不是真正的问题。如果对方会说：“不不不不不。这不是问题所在。问题是……”，并且给出他们对问题的描述，那才是你真正需要关注的。所以即使你和100个人交流，但如果你实际只和20个陌生人交流，你就能验证这个问题是否真实存在。

（00:10:23）：听着，这不是成功的唯一途径，对吧？看看世界上最成功的产品之一——iPhone，对吧？你会问自己，他们刚开始时到底遇到了什么问题？答案是，他们刚开始时并没有问题。当时已经有智能手机了，人们对它们也非常满意。所以有时候我们需要发明全新的东西，但解决问题才是创造价值最简单的方法。

It doesn't matter if I'm not that passionate about it."
turns.zh: 选择一个要解决的问题的另一个要素，就是你说你要爱上这个问题。就是对解决这个问题感到兴奋。很多时候，你会发现有些问题并不能让你兴奋，比如房地产软件，但你发现了一个大问题。相对于“哦，哇。这是一个巨大的商业机会。我必须抓住它。即使我对它不感兴趣也没关系。”这种想法，个人对这个问题的热情和兴奋感有多重要呢？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Fall in love, right? This is really passionate. Really, really passionate. Look, the journey is really hard and complex and long and so you have to be in love in order to go into this journey because otherwise it's not going to be successful. You really want to be passionate. If you're not passionate about the problem, even though that the problem might be real and big and significant, there is not enough drive, there is not enough internal drive to take you through the hardship of the journey, and so you need to be passionate. You need to fall in love. You personally need to fall in love with the problem. And then actually what you're trying to do is engage everyone else to fall in love with the same problem, to go into this journey, into this path and follow your leadership there.
turns.zh: 爱上它，对吧？这真的很热情。非常、非常热情。看，这段旅程真的很艰难、复杂、漫长，所以你必须满怀热爱才能踏上这段旅程，否则它不会成功。你真的需要充满热情。如果你对这个问题不感兴趣，即使这个问题可能很真实、很重大、很重要，但你没有足够的动力，没有足够的内在驱动力来度过这段艰难的旅程，所以你需要充满热情。你需要爱上它。你个人需要爱上这个问题。而实际上，你要做的就是让其他人也爱上同一个问题，一起踏上这段旅程，走上这条道路，并跟随你的领导。

turns.zh: 有没有你经历过的转型案例，让你意识到问题并没有你想象的那么大，或者意识到还有更大的问题？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So actually there are many, right? So Oversee deals with maybe biggest secret in travel industry. What happened to airfare after you booked your flight? Now you have no idea because you never compare prices after you met the reservation. But you know that airfare is going up and down all the time. It's going up and down before you are making the reservation and keep on going up and down after you're making the reservation. So if this is the price that you paid and this is cancellation fees, if the price drops here, you can rebook the same flight at the cheaper price.
turns.zh: 事实上，类似的情况有很多，对吧？Oversee 致力于解决旅游行业中最隐蔽的秘密——你预订航班后，机票价格到底会怎样变化？现在你可能一无所知，因为预订后你从未对比过价格。但你知道机票价格一直在波动——在预订前价格就起起伏伏，预订后更是如此。所以，如果这是你支付的价格，而这里是取消费用，如果价格下跌，你就可以以更低的价格重新预订同样的航班。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Genius.
turns.zh: 真是天才想法。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: If you would only keep on comparing prices after that, right? So we started this company that is actually monitoring your own itinerary and we realized that this is going to be huge benefits to travelers and we started that as a B2C company, direct to consumers, and we realized that even though the people really care, they are not willing to take the action that is required, and we ended up with doing that for corporates, and in corporates there are very simple ways for them to engage that automatically, so automatic rebooking and so forth, and we can save corporates about 10% of the travel budget that goes directly to bottom line. So we started that as a B2C and then we realized that this is way harder than we think it is, and we ended up with converting that into B2B, which turns out to be very successful for us. And so occasionally there are companies that you start your journey with one perception and you change that and that will happen multiple times.
turns.zh: 如果你能在预订后持续对比价格，对吧？所以我们创立了这家公司，实时监控用户的行程安排。我们意识到这对旅行者将带来巨大好处，于是以B2C模式直接面向消费者提供服务。但我们发现，即便人们对此很关注，却不愿采取必要行动。最终我们将业务转向企业客户，为他们提供自动改签等便捷服务，帮助企业节省约10%的差旅预算，直接提升利润。因此，我们最初是B2C模式，但后来发现其难度超出预期，于是转型为B2B模式，结果大获成功。有时候创业之路会充满曲折，初衷和最终成果可能大相径庭。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. I want to, before I move on to, I'm kind of thinking about this in the phases of starting a company. So we're talking right now about coming up with the idea that you want to commit to. A lot of people that want to start companies are not sure how to find a great idea, so the core advice you're sharing is find something, find a problem, and fall in love with solving that problem in whatever way you can. Do you have any other advice for helping somebody find a problem and finding a startup idea? Where do you find startup ideas? What do you find? What does work for you mostly?
turns.zh: 这真是个绝佳案例。我想接着探讨一下创业公司的创立阶段。目前我们讨论的是如何确定要投入精力的创业方向。许多想创业的人不知道如何找到好的创意，你能否给出核心建议：发现问题，找到痛点，并全力以赴解决它？对于寻找创业点子，你有什么建议？从哪里能获得灵感？哪些方法对你最有效？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So for me, it's usually personal frustration that leads me to start to think about it, whether or not we can change it. I hate traffic jams, right? I hate leaving money on the table, right? So there are many things that I ran into and I get frustrated and I tell myself, "No, no, no. There must be a different way to do that." But in general, look, the problem itself needs to start from you, right? Something that really bothers you, something that you care about, and then it's the validations of the problem that you speak with many people, try to realize. Now if you'll tell me, oh, this is a B2B, then speak with many businesses, right? Speak with those that you believe actually do have this problem and I understand their perception. (00:15:13): Once you validate that, then there are few things that you need to realize. One is about the journey itself. This is going to be a multi-dimensional journey. It's going to be at least three dimensions and maybe fourth, right? So the three dimensions, one of them is it's going to be a roller coaster journey with ups and downs and ups and downs. And look, if you'll tell me that all the businesses in the world have ups and downs, I agree, but the frequency of those when you are building a startup? Way higher. I think that I heard the best quote on that from Ben Horowitz, Ben Horowitz from Andreessen Horowitz venture capital firm, and before that he used to be a CEO of a startup and he was asked whether or not he was sleeping well at night and he said, "Oh, yeah, I slept like a baby. I woke up every two hours and cried." And that's really the reality of that. The frequency of the differences are so dramatic that there is nothing compared to that, a roller coaster journey. (00:16:17): It's also a journey of failures. Look, we are trying to build something new that no one did before, and even though that we think that we know exactly what we are doing, we don't. So we try. We try one thing and it doesn't work. We try another thing and it doesn't work. Or if we keep on trying different things until we find one thing that does work. Now, if you realize that this is going to be a journey of failures, then there are two immediate conclusions. The first one is that if you're afraid to fail, then in reality you already failed because you are not going to try. Albert Einstein used to say that if you haven't failed, that because you haven't tried new things before. If you're going to try new things, you will fail. Michael Jordan used to say that, "I've failed over and over and over and over again and this is what made me successful." And so this is the first conclusion. (00:17:07): The second conclusion is that you really want to fail fast. Just think about it, right? If you fail fast, you still have plenty of time to try another attempt and build another version of the product. Try another go-to-market approach. Try a different business model so you still have plenty of time to make more and more and more attempts, and the more attempts that you have, you simply increase the likelihood of being successful. Just think that you play basketball, right, and you try to score from half court. If you have one shot and you are not Steph Curry, you are very likely to miss. But if you actually have a lot of shots, one of them you're going to make. That's it. Just think about it. The biggest enemy of good enough is perfect. You don't need to be perfect. You need to be good enough in order to win the market, and the way that you are going to become good enough, by the way, is really simple. You start with not good enough and you iterate and iterate and iterate until you become good enough and then you'll win. (00:18:10): The third dimension is that this is going to be long journey. Very long. Way longer than you think it is. And the longest part of it is until you figure out product market fit, and product market fit goes into the different phases of building a company. To a certain extent, I would say, look, the difference between a corporate and a startup is that a corporate knows this is our value proposition, this is the product that we are selling, this is the pricing of this product that we are selling, this is the target audience, this is how we are going to sell them, this is how we going to the market, and all we have to do is keep on executing and hopefully nothing will change over the period of time. When you start as a startup, you don't have a product. You don't know what's the business model. You don't know what people are going to pay you for. You don't know how to grow your business, and you need to figure out all of those, and this is going to be a long journey. (00:19:11): Now, the longest part is usually figuring out product market fit and product market fit is really simple. That means that you create value to your customers. If you do not figure out product market fit, you will die. As simple as that. You never heard of a company that did not figure out product market fit. They simply died. That's it. Now, once they do, and for a second I want you to think of, with all the applications that you're using every day, right? From searching Google, using Waze, WhatsApp, Facebook, Netflix, Uber, whatever it is, and ask yourself what is the difference between any of those today and the first time that you have used that? And the answer is that there is no difference. We are searching Google today the same way that we searched Google for the first time in our life. We're using Waze today the same way that we used Waze for the first time in their life. So once a company figure out product market fit, they don't change their product anymore because this is the value that they created to the customers and you don't want to change that. (00:20:14): What we don't know is how long did it take them to get to this point, right? Beforehand we never heard of them and after that they don't change that anymore. It's a matter of years. For Waze, it was four years. For Microsoft, it was five years. For Netflix, it was 10 years. Now if you'll tell me, "Oh, today is very different. ChatGPT just started a year ago." No, they're seven years old. It took them six years until you heard about them for the first time in your life. So it does take time to create value and this is something that is really significant. Now, at the end of the day, product market fit have one metric. One metric. That's it. Retention. That's really simple. If you create value, they will come back. If they're not coming back, that means that you are not creating value. Now think about your episodes, right, of this podcast, right? Most of your listeners are returning, right? Because you create value for them and they are coming back. That's it.
turns.zh:
对我来说，通常是个人挫败感促使我开始思考这个问题——无论我们能否改变现状。我讨厌堵车，对吧？我讨厌把钱白白浪费掉，对吧？所以我遇到过很多这样的情况，然后感到沮丧，告诉自己：“不，不，不。一定有更好的解决办法。” 但总的来说，问题本身必须从你自己出发，对吧？那些真正困扰你、你真正关心的东西，然后通过与许多人交流、不断验证来认识这个问题。现在如果你告诉我，哦，这是一个B2B业务，那就去和许多企业交流，对吧？和那些你认为确实存在这个问题的企业交流，我理解他们的看法。（00:15:13）：一旦你验证了这一点，那么你需要意识到几件事。首先是关于旅程本身。这将是一次多维度的旅程。至少有三个维度，甚至可能是四个，对吧？这三个维度之一，就是像过山车一样的起起落落。听着，如果你告诉我世界上所有企业都有起起落落，我同意，但当你创办初创公司时，这种频率要高得多。我记得本·霍洛维茨（Andreessen Horowitz风险投资公司的创始人）说过的最好的观点，他曾担任初创公司的CEO，当被问及是否晚上睡得好时，他回答：“哦，是的，我睡得像婴儿一样，每两个小时就醒来哭一次。” 这就是现实。频繁的波动如此剧烈，简直无法比拟，这就是过山车般的旅程。（00:16:17）：这也是一次失败的旅程。看，我们试图创造前所未有的新事物，即使我们自认为很清楚自己在做什么，但其实并非如此。所以我们尝试。尝试一种方法不成功，再尝试另一种。或者不断尝试不同的方法，直到找到有效的方案。现在，如果你意识到这将是一次失败的旅程，那么有两个直接的结论。第一个结论是，如果你害怕失败，那么实际上你已经失败了，因为你根本不会尝试。爱因斯坦曾说过，如果你没有失败，那是因为你从未尝试过新事物。如果你要尝试新事物，你就必将失败。迈克尔·乔丹曾说：“我一次又一次地失败，这才成就了我的成功。” 这就是第一个结论。（00:17:07）：第二个结论是，你真的希望快速失败。想想看，对吧？快速失败意味着你还有充足的时间进行下一次尝试，打造另一个版本的产品，尝试另一种市场推广策略，尝试不同的商业模式，这样你就有足够的时间进行更多尝试，而尝试次数越多，你成功的可能性就越大。想想打篮球吧，对吧？如果你只投一次球，而你又不是斯蒂芬·库里，那很可能投不进。但如果你有很多次投篮机会，其中总会有一次命中的。就是这样。想想看，好是敌人完美。你不需要完美。你只需要足够好就能赢得市场，而要达到足够好其实很简单。先从不完美开始，
不断迭代、迭代、再迭代，直到你足够优秀，然后你就能赢了。（00:18:10）：第三个维度是这将是一段漫长的旅程。非常漫长。远比你想象的要长得多。而最漫长的部分是直到你找到产品与市场的契合点，而产品与市场的契合点又分成公司发展的不同阶段。在某种程度上，我想说，企业和初创公司的区别在于，企业知道我们的价值主张是什么，我们销售的产品是什么，我们销售产品的定价是什么，我们的目标客户是谁，我们将如何向他们销售产品，我们将如何进入市场，而我们只需要继续执行，希望在一段时间内不会有任何变化。当你以初创公司的身份起步时，你没有产品。你不知道商业模式是什么。你不知道人们会为你支付什么费用。你不知道如何发展业务，而你需要弄清楚所有这些问题，这将是一段漫长的旅程。（00:19:11）：现在，最漫长的部分通常是找到产品与市场的契合点，而产品与市场的契合点其实很简单。这意味着你为客户创造价值。如果你没有找到产品与市场的契合点，你就会失败。就这么简单。你从未听说过没有找到产品与市场的契合点的公司。他们就这样失败了。就是这样。现在，一旦他们做到了，接下来我想让你想一想，你每天使用的所有应用程序，对吧？从搜索谷歌、使用Waze、WhatsApp、Facebook、Netflix、Uber等等，想一想如今这些应用与你第一次使用它们时有什么不同？答案是没有任何不同。我们今天搜索谷歌的方式和我们人生中第一次搜索谷歌是一样的。我们今天使用Waze的方式和我们人生中第一次使用Waze是一样的。所以，一旦一家公司找到了产品与市场的契合点，他们就不会再改变产品了，因为这就是他们为客户创造的价值，而你不想改变这一点。（00:20:14）：但我们不知道他们花了多长时间才走到这一步，对吧？在此之前，我们从未听说过他们，而在此之后，他们就再也不变了。这需要数年时间。Waze用了四年。微软用了五年。Netflix用了10年。现在如果你告诉我，"哦，今天情况很不同。ChatGPT一年前才刚推出。"不，它已经有七年历史了。直到你第一次听说它时已经过了六年。所以创造价值确实需要时间，而这一点非常重要。现在，说到最后，产品与市场的契合点只有一个指标。只有一个指标。就是留存率。这很简单。如果你创造了价值，他们就会回来。如果他们不回来，这意味着你没有创造价值。现在想想你的播客剧集，对吧？你的大多数听众都会回来，对吧？因为你为他们创造了价值，他们就会回来。就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 100%. Every single one, every episode.
turns.zh: 100%。每一项，每一集都是如此。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Occasionally there are new one, right?
turns.zh: 偶尔会有新内容出现，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's new ones coming in all the time.
turns.zh: 而且新内容层出不穷。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: [inaudible 00:21:32]. By the way, this is one thing that some businesses don't realize, whether or not their customers are going to be new customers or returning customers, and in many cases they simply fail to realize that upfront and the result is that they are not building the right go-to-market strategy.
turns.zh: [00:21:32语音不清]。顺便说一句，有些企业没有意识到这一点——无论客户是新客户还是回头客——很多时候他们事先根本没有意识到这一点，最终导致他们制定了错误的市场策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We covered a lot of ground there. That was amazing. I'm going to follow a number of threads of things you just touched on. You talked about product market fit briefly. What was the moment you felt product market fit with Waze? I don't know if I've ever heard that story.
turns.zh: 我们已经讨论了很多内容，真是太棒了。我打算追踪你刚刚提到的几个要点。你简要谈到了产品与市场的契合度。你什么时候意识到Waze与市场契合的？我不知道自己是否听过这个故事。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: We started in Israel and Israel is a small place and we ended up with being very successful in Israel and then we said, "Wait a minute. Waze crowdsource all the data, right?" Not just the traffic information and speed cams and so forth, but also the map data itself, so we can start from a blank page. And the users while they drive, they create the map and they create traffic information and so forth. And so we figure out that we can start anywhere and we made Waze global at the end of 2009 and we expect that to work the same way that it did in Israel, but it didn't. It was not good enough. It was not good enough in the U.S. It was not good enough in Western Europe. It was not good enough in Latin America, it was not good enough in Asia. It was not good enough anywhere that matters, right? (00:22:57): It was actually good enough in about four places. In the Czech Republic, in Slovakia, in Latvia and Ecuador, and that's about it. Rest of the world not good enough. So what we did is we spoke with the drivers. Look, they wanted us to be successful. We basically said the drivers are going to fight traffic jams together, so common enemy, togetherness, all goodness. Everyone wanted that to work, right? So people downloaded the app and it simply was not good enough. So they churned, right, because if it's not good enough, you're not coming back. We spoke with them. We asked them what didn't work for them. They told us because they wanted it to work, and we built the next version addressing everything that they've told us, and we know that this is it, and it's not. So we doing it all over again. We speak with the drivers. We ask them what didn't work for them, they tell us. Now we build the next version and now we have the conviction that it's going to work and it's not. Journey of failures. (00:23:58): Iteration after iteration after iteration after iteration. More than a year of iterations until beginning of 2011 that we actually started to see that working, and then it's in multiple places. In the U.S., one metropolitan after the other, right? Los Angeles first and then San Francisco and then Washington D.C. and Chicago and New York and Atlanta and so forth. In Europe, one country after the other. Italy first and then France and Netherlands and Sweden and Spain and one country after the other. In Latin America, one country after the other. Colombia first and then Chile and then Brazil and then Mexico and then rest of Latin America. In Asia, multiple countries one after the other. Not all of them, by the way. Not all of them. Japan is a very good example where it didn't work and it will never work. Waze crowdsourced the information, right? Which basically says that as soon as we get to the level of good enough, then we are good enough. (00:25:01): House numbering plan. In the U.S., it's really simple, right? Every block is a hundreth numbers, right? And so if I have the map, I can actually count the number of blocks and take you to approximate the right location even if I don't have exactly all the house numbers there. Most of the western world, it's a geographical order. So in Israel, this is going to be sequential order, odd number on one side of the street, even number on the other side of the street starting from one until the end of the street and so forth, so it's enough that I will have few house numbers that I can actually take you to the right place. (00:25:38): In the UK, house number starts on one side off the street and then on the other side they are coming back, right? And so there is an order. In Japan, it's chronological order. The oldest house in the neighborhood is house number one.
turns.zh:
我们的业务始于以色列——这个国家面积不大，但我们在那里取得了巨大成功。随后，我们意识到："等等，Waze的所有数据都是用户众包的，对吧？"不只是交通信息、测速摄像头之类的数据，地图数据本身也是如此——这意味着我们可以从零开始。但当用户在开车时创建地图和交通信息时，我们发现这个模式在其他地区行不通。2009年底，我们试图将Waze全球化，却发现无论是在美国、西欧、拉丁美洲还是亚洲，都达不到预期的效果。

（00:22:57）：实际上有四个地方做得不错——捷克共和国、斯洛伐克、拉脱维亚和厄瓜多尔，其他地区都不行。于是我们开始倾听用户意见。他们希望我们成功，我们提出"用户共同对抗交通拥堵"，强调团结协作。但即便如此，用户还是流失了。因为产品不达标，用户自然不会回来。我们反复沟通，了解用户痛点并优化产品，但结果依然不尽如人意。于是我们又从头开始，重新与用户对话，倾听他们的反馈，优化产品，最终发现方向正确，却又偏离轨道。

（00:23:58）：一次又一次的迭代。2011年初，产品终于在多个地区实现突破：美国从洛杉矶到旧金山，再到华盛顿、芝加哥、纽约和亚特兰大；欧洲从意大利到法国、荷兰、瑞典、西班牙；拉丁美洲从哥伦比亚到智利、巴西、墨西哥；亚洲多个国家……但日本是个例外，那里永远无法成功。

（00:25:01）：地址编号体系的差异。美国很简单，每个街区百号起；而以色列是顺序编号，奇数在一侧，偶数在另一侧；英国则先左后右；日本则完全无序。
顺序。附近最古老的房子是1号房。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: And then the house number two can be miles away, but it's the second oldest house in the neighborhood and so you have to have all the house numbers unless... Until then you are not good enough. And crowdsource is, if you need perfect information, crowdsource may not be the right way to do that.
turns.zh: 然后，第二栋房子可能相隔数英里之遥，但它是附近第二古老的房子，所以你必须标注所有房号，除非……在此之前，你做得还不够好。众包服务是，如果你需要完美信息，众包可能不是正确的解决方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to close the loop on this question, when you were launching these markets and it wasn't working, were you actually looking at retention at that point, and if so, was there a number you were looking for? Or was it more qualitative like it's just taken off off into the right. Like where were you actually watching back in the early days?
turns.zh: 最后来回答这个问题：当你推出这些市场但效果不佳时，你当时是否关注用户留存率？如果是，有没有具体的数据目标？还是说更多是定性分析，比如用户自然而然地流失了？在早期阶段，你是如何监控用户行为的？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: That was easier for us because we tried to compare everything to Israel, so we looked at the frequency of use or when our people are coming back. How long does it take them until the next try and until the next try. And in generally speaking, if you look at something that have high frequency of use, then you will be looking at three-month retentions of 30, 40, 50% is actually pretty good indication. But usually what would happen is that you would know when they convert and that's going to be after the third or the fourth time, and if they're not getting to the fourth time, then they are basically saying, "Okay. We gave it a try. We really like this story. We gave it another try, and it's not good enough."
turns.zh: 这对我们来说相对容易，因为我们试图将一切与以色列进行比较，所以我们关注使用频率或用户回访时间。用户需要多长时间才会再次尝试？一般来说，如果某项服务使用频率很高，那么三个月内30%、40%、50%的留存率实际上是一个很好的指标。但通常情况下，用户会在第三次或第四次尝试后才完成转化，如果他们连第四次都没到，那就意味着他们会说：“好吧，我们试过了，我们很喜欢这个产品，但还是不够好。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a cool heuristic. Do you find that that is useful for other startups, consumer-type startups or is that just something you think specific to Waze at that point, this idea of coming back for the third time?
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的启发。你觉得这对其他初创公司，特别是消费者类型的初创公司也有用吗？还是说这只是Waze特有的思路？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: It's really depending on the frequency of use, right? If I will tell you that I have a startup that helps you to file your tax returns in three minutes, then okay, that's absolutely amazing, but you are only going to do that, next time is next year. By the way, we did have a startup that was doing that. It's still a little bit up and running, but that was really frustrating because the tax authority shut us down.
turns.zh: 这真的取决于使用频率，对吧？比如，如果我告诉你我有一个初创公司，能帮助用户在三分钟内完成纳税申报，那当然很棒，但用户可能只会用一次，明年再试一次。顺便说一下，我们确实有过这样一个初创公司。它目前还在运营中，但因为税务部门把我们关停了，所以进展很不顺利。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You got to fall in with the problem. You got to power through that. Just change the government. Just kidding. The story you told of Waze and iterating is a really good example of falling in love with the problem. You're really passionate about. I want to solve traffic, I hate traffic. By the way, what it made me think about a little bit is Elon, when he hated traffic, he built the boring company and built tunnels underground, and your solution to hate traffic is I'm going to build Waze in a soft wrap.
turns.zh: 你必须深入到问题核心，必须坚持不懈地解决问题。比如，改变政府政策？开玩笑的。你讲的Waze迭代的故事，是一个真正爱上问题的绝佳例子。你对解决交通问题充满热情。我讨厌交通！顺便说一下，这让我想起了埃隆，他讨厌交通，所以创办了无聊公司，挖地道。而你解决交通问题的办法是开发Waze这样的应用。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: We start Waze with the vision that we are going to help people to avoid traffic jams. Now the reality is that there are more traffic jams today than there were in 2007. Obviously, number one, I'm not done. And number two, if you ask people what is the value of Waze, then it's not about avoiding traffic. It's about creating certainty and certainty is way higher value than saving time. So you know exactly when you're going to get there and this is a way higher value. And by the way, we learned that in the U.S. market when we spoke with people. They told us, "If I am living in Cupertino and I need to drive up to San Francisco and I can take 101 or 280, I don't really want to change my route unless there is something dramatic, but what I really want to know is how long it's going to take me. So I'm going to stay on the 101. I'm not going to get into service road. I'm not going to take El Camino Real. I'm not going to try something else. I'm going to stay on the 101. Just let me know how long it's going to take." So certainty creates way more value than saving time.
turns.zh: 我们创立Waze时，怀揣着帮助人们避开交通拥堵的愿景。但如今的现实是，2017年交通拥堵的情况比2007年更为严重。显然，首先，我尚未达成目标。其次，如果你问人们Waze的价值所在，答案并非是帮助避开交通拥堵，而是为用户提供确定性。确定性带来的价值远超节省时间。用户能准确预知到达时间，这才是更高的价值。顺便说一句，我们在美国市场调研时发现，当地居民表示：“如果我住在库比蒂诺，需要开车去旧金山，可以选择101号公路或280号公路，除非遇到极端情况，我不会特意改道。但我真正关心的还是通行时长。所以我会继续沿着101号公路行驶，不走辅路，也不绕行El Camino Real公路。只要能告知我预计到达时间，我就愿意坚持原路。”可见，确定性带来的价值远超节省时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk through a couple other of the chapters in your book. So chapter four is around the different phases of a startup journey and your core advice is that it's important to focus on one thing at a time in each of these phases, and the first phase, you call it the all over the place phase, I think, or yeah, the all over phase, and the idea is you need to get out of that as soon as you can and then focus. Can you just kind of talk through these different phases and what you think people do wrong along the phases? Maybe they get them wrong or they focus on the wrong things in each phase.
turns.zh: 接下来，我想探讨一下您书中其他章节的内容。第四章主要讲述初创企业的不同发展阶段，您给出的核心建议是，在每个阶段都专注于一件事至关重要。第一阶段您称之为“杂乱无章阶段”，我想是这样的，或者可以说是“混乱期”。关键是尽快摆脱这种状态，然后专注于核心任务。您能否详细解析这些不同阶段，并谈谈人们在每个阶段可能犯的错误？比如，他们可能误解了阶段的本质，或者在每个阶段都关注了错误的重点。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So initially you think about your new idea from multiple perspective, right? This is the problem. This is how this solution is going to look like. This is what I'm going to do next year. This is my 10 years vision. This is my business model and so forth. So you think about everything, but you actually need to execute only one thing. Now this one thing is figuring out product market fit. It's not one thing, right? Wait a minute. You also need to build an organization and you want that organization to be something that you really like and so there are a lot of operational stuff, but you need to figure out product market fit. As we said earlier, if you don't figure out product market fit, you will die. If you do, then you get to live and die another day and the other day is whether or not you're going to figure out how to grow your business and whether or not you're going to figure out your business model. (00:31:11): Now the good news is that I will tell you that if you create value, you will figure out a business model, at least for the people that you create value for them. They are most likely willing to pay. Now in general, I'm not saying that this is the only business model that is viable, but if you create value, you will figure out a business model. But figuring out a business model is a journey by itself, and guess what? It's going to be a long roller coaster journey of failures. When we started Waze, we thought that we're going to sell map data and traffic information and we ended up with doing advertisement. Very different business model. Because we realized that it's not for us. It's too long sales cycles. We were very mobile internet dynamic company and selling to government is not exactly what we wanted to do, and so we ended up with a different business model, but with a lot of reasoning why this is the right business model for us. (00:32:14): And figuring out growth, look, if I would ask a hundred people on the street, how did you hear about Waze? They, 95 of them, if not 99 of them, will tell me, "Someone told me." Word-of-mouth, right? So everyone wants to have word-of-mouth. Word-of-mouth you can only have if you have high frequency of use. If you're doing tax returns once a year, even if you really like the experience, then once a year you're going to tell someone else. If you're using Waze every day, then every day you have an opportunity to tell someone else. So word-of-mouth, even though that everyone would like that, it's only going to happen if you have high frequency of use. (00:33:01): So those phases requires different focus of the company, right? Initially if you focus on product market fit, then you don't need sales. You have no product to sell. You don't need business development. You don't need even marketing. You need product. You need developers and you need product lead to define the product and lead through the iterations of the product until we get to the level that it's good enough. Once you get there, you shift gears. If the product doesn't change, if we search Google the same way that we searched Google for the first time in our life, then the product development is now not going to be focused about value creation. It's going to be focused about either figuring out business model or figuring out scale, and the entire company shift gears and move to a different phase. (00:33:54): Now, this is really hard. Just think about it. If up until now the product development group was the only things that matters, all of a sudden we think about marketing now because we are now in the go-to-market phase that this is the most important thing of the company. Occasionally I found companies that have challenging and shifting gears so they didn't figure out where the clutch is and you have to because otherwise you're stuck in the previous phase that you kind of finished that journey. This journey is nearly done and you need to shift gears, and if you don't do that, then you get stuck. If you do that, if you try to do multiple things at the same time, you will fail. Focus is not about what we are doing, it's about what we are not doing. These are the hard decisions.
turns.zh:
起初，你会从多个角度思考自己的新想法，对吧？但这恰恰是问题所在。这项解决方案最终会是什么样子？明年我要做什么？我的十年愿景是什么？我的商业模式又是什么？如此种种，你把一切都想了一遍，但实际上你只需要专注于一件事——那就是明确产品与市场的契合度。这不是唯一需要关注的点，对吧？等等，还有组织架构的搭建，你希望这个组织能符合你的理想，所以还有很多运营层面的工作，但核心在于产品与市场的契合度。正如我们之前所说，如果不解决这个问题，你的项目就会夭折。若成功解决，你就能继续生存并迎来下一阶段的挑战——如何实现业务增长和商业模式的创新。（00:31:11）好消息是，只要你能创造价值，就一定能找到商业模式，至少能为你的核心用户群体创造价值。他们很可能愿意为此付费。当然，我并不是说这是唯一可行的商业模式，但只要你能创造价值，商业模式自然会浮现。但探索商业模式本身就是一条漫长曲折的失败之路。我们创立Waze时，原计划销售地图数据和交通信息，最后却转型做广告。这完全不同的商业模式背后，是我们意识到这条路不适合我们——销售周期太长。我们本是移动互联网时代的活力公司，与政府合作并非我们的初衷，最终我们找到了适合自己的商业模式，并为此进行了充分论证。（00:32:14）至于增长策略，试问街头100个人，你是如何得知Waze的？95个甚至99个都会回答：“别人告诉我的。”口口相传，对吧？所以大家都渴望口碑传播。但要实现口碑传播，前提是产品的高频使用。假如你每年只报税一次，即便体验再好，也只有一年一次机会告诉别人。而Waze每天都在被使用，每天都是传播机会。因此，口碑传播虽是理想状态，但必须建立在高频使用基础上。（00:33:01）不同阶段对公司的关注点不同。对吧？初期专注产品与市场的契合度，不需要销售团队，因为没有产品可卖。不需要业务拓展团队，也不需要营销团队——只需要产品、开发者和产品负责人，定义产品并推动迭代，直到产品足够完善。达到这个阶段后，就需要转换思路。如果产品不迭代，比如你搜索Google的方式和初次使用时完全相同，那么产品开发的核心就从价值创造转向商业模式探索或规模化扩张，整个公司随之进入新阶段。（00:33:54）这真的很困难。试想一下，如果此前产品开发团队是唯一的核心部门，现在我们却要考虑营销，因为我们进入了市场推广阶段。
这是公司最重要的事情。我偶尔会遇到那些面临挑战、需要转变策略的公司，他们却始终找不到关键节点，而你必须找到，否则就会被困在前一个阶段，无法完成整个历程。现在这段旅程即将结束，你必须转换思路。如果不这样做，就会停滞不前。如果你试图同时做多件事，必将以失败告终。专注力不在于我们正在做什么，而在于我们不该做什么。这些都是艰难的抉择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. So the four phases, just to briefly summarize, it's kind of like come up with the idea, find product market fit, then it's a question of should you keep focusing on growth or should you figure out the business model before focusing heavily on growth? In your advice, it sounds like if it's high frequency, word-of-mouth driven, focus on growth and then you figure out business model later. If not, figure out how you're going to make money and then figure out growth.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点。简单来说，四个阶段就是：首先构思创意，找到产品与市场的契合点，然后要考虑是继续专注增长，还是先理清商业模式再全力推进增长？在你的建议中，我理解到如果产品使用频率高、靠口碑驱动，就应该先专注增长，再逐步完善商业模式；反之，就得先想清楚如何盈利，再着手增长。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Exactly. Because if you have high frequency of use, you will end up with growth coming by itself, right, for word-of-mouth, and therefore you should do that at the beginning. If you don't have high frequency of use, you are sentenced to acquire users or customers all of your lifetime. If this is the case, then you really want to figure out the business model before you start and go and do that.
turns.zh: 确实如此。因为如果产品使用频率高，那么口碑传播带来的增长会自然而然地发生，所以你应该在初期就着重打造这一点。若频率不高，那你就注定要终身去获取用户或客户了。在这种情况下，你确实需要在启动前先确定商业模式再行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really helpful. I think actually a counter example to your point about how frequency of use is necessary for word-of-mouth growth is Airbnb. Something like 70% of Airbnb growth is word-of-mouth and frequency of use is actually really low. It's like once or twice a year. I wonder if it's because the experience is so unique and special that it still works and enough people travel enough times, slash if it was a higher frequency, it would've grown even faster, I imagine.
turns.zh: 这点确实很有启发。不过Airbnb或许是个反例。Airbnb 70%的增长来自口碑传播，而其使用频率实际上很低，用户平均每年使用一两次。我好奇是否因为其独特体验太吸引人，所以即便频率不高也能成功？如果频率更高，增长速度会更快吧？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: High frequency of use is the simplest way for word-of-mouth. The other thing is coolness. If it's really cool, then you'll tell more people, and Airbnb was really cool at the beginning of the journey, so now everyone knows about Airbnb, but when they started that was way cheaper and really unique experience than hotels.
turns.zh: 高频使用是口碑传播最简单的方式。另一个关键因素是产品的“酷感”。如果产品足够酷，人们就会更乐意传播。Airbnb在初期就非常酷，所以现在大家都知道它，但刚起步时价格更低，体验比酒店更独特。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's still actually mostly word-of-mouth. I think it was probably higher initially, but it's still almost 70, 80% driven by word-of-mouth. So it's still cool enough. Good for them. You have a couple of quotes that I wanted to share, which are along the lines of things you shared. One is just, you have this kind of, what's the most important stage at a company? They all are, but one at a time. I love that line. The other is the main thing is to keep the main thing the main thing. The same advice you just shared. Just like focus. So you're in the PM, product market fit phase. Focus on that. Don't think about growth yet. Don't think about business model yet necessarily. I know investors are going to push you to figure these things out and you'll have to have some story of like, "Here's how it might make money. Here's how we think we're going to grow." Right? You need to think about that a little bit, but maybe don't make that the focus.
turns.zh: 口碑传播仍然是核心驱动力。虽然初期频率可能更高，但现在仍有70%-80%的增长来自口碑传播。这说明产品足够酷，值得点赞。你分享的几句名言很贴切，比如“公司最重要的阶段是什么？每个阶段都很重要，但每个阶段只专注一件事。”还有“最重要的是专注最重要的事。”这些建议和你的观点不谋而合。比如在产品市场契合阶段，专注于此，先别考虑增长和商业模式。我知道投资者会催促你，但你需要先有清晰的思路，比如“这里有盈利模式”、“我们如何实现增长”等。这些可以作为备选方案，但不应成为核心关注点。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So this is one of the areas that investors don't like to hear the truth, right? The truth is that I don't know how I'm going to bring the users. I will figure that out once I get there, but the reality is that right now I don't know, but they don't want to hear that. What they want to hear is that, "Oh, I know exactly how I'm going to bring them." And what I will say is that I know exactly where I'm going to start my experiments, but most of the investors would like to see a coherent story that makes sense, right? This is our business model. This is how we going to make money. This is what we're going to sell. This is how much they're going to pay. This is why it's a simple business model and these are the comparable to this business model.
turns.zh: 嗯，投资者们不喜欢听真话，这就是其中一个原因吧。事实上，我并不知道该如何吸引用户。等我到了那一步再想办法，但现实是，我现在确实不知道该怎么做，但他们不想听这个。他们想听的是：“哦，我完全知道该怎么吸引用户。” 而我要说的是，我确实知道从哪里开始实验，但大多数投资者希望看到一个连贯、合理的商业计划，对吧？这是我们的商业模式，这是我们如何盈利的，这是我们要销售的产品，用户愿意为此支付多少钱。这就是一个简单的商业模式，也是与之相似的其他商业模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. But investors have the final word, unfortunately. They decide if they want to invest or not, and so if your story is not compelling, they're going to be like, "All right. We'll find someone else."
turns.zh: 是啊，但很遗憾，投资者说了算。他们决定是否投资，所以如果你讲的故事不够吸引人，他们就会说：“好吧，我们再找别人吧。”

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: You know, it's seasonality, right? There are periods of time that raising capital is easier and then many of the entrepreneurs will be choosers are not beggars, and there are periods of time that is that way around, and most of the entrepreneurs will be beggars and not choosers.
turns.zh: 你知道的，这和季节性有关，对吧？有些时候融资更容易，而很多创业者会成为挑剔者而非乞丐；有些时候情况则相反，大多数创业者会成为乞丐而非挑剔者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Imagine a place where you can find all your potential customers and get your message in front of them in a cost-efficient way. If you're a B2B business, that place exists, and it's called LinkedIn. LinkedIn Ads allows you to build the right relationships, drive results, and reach your customers in a respectful environment. Two of my portfolio companies, Webflow and Census are LinkedIn success stories. Census had a 10x increase in pipeline with the LinkedIn startup team. For Webflow, after ramping up on LinkedIn in Q4, they had the highest marketing source revenue quarter to date. With LinkedIn Ads, you'll have direct access to and can build relationships with decision makers including 950 million members, 180 million senior execs and over 10 million C-level executives. You'll be able to drive results with targeting and measurement tools built specifically for B2B. (00:39:24): In tech, LinkedIn generated two to five x higher return on ad spend than any other social media platforms. Audiences on LinkedIn have two times the buying power of the average web audience, and you'll work with a partner who respects the B2B world you operate in. Make B2B marketing everything it can be and get $100 credit on your next campaign. Just go to LinkedIn.com/podLenny to claim your credit. That's LinkedIn.com/podLenny. Terms and conditions apply. (00:39:52): Let's actually talk about fundraising as a topic I wanted to spend a little time on. How much money have you raised for the companies that you've started total, roughly?
turns.zh: 想象一个地方，你可以在那里找到所有潜在客户，并以低成本的方式将信息传达给他们。如果你做的是B2B业务，这个地方就存在，它叫做LinkedIn。LinkedIn广告让你能够在一个尊重的环境中建立正确的关系、推动成果并接触客户。我的两个投资组合公司Webflow和Census都是LinkedIn的成功案例。Census与LinkedIn的创业团队合作后，其销售线索增长了10倍。对于Webflow而言，在第四季度加强LinkedIn营销后，他们创下了迄今为止营销收入最高的季度纪录。通过LinkedIn广告，你将直接接触并与决策者建立关系，包括9.5亿会员、1800万高级管理人员和超过1000万C级高管。你将能够利用专为B2B打造的定向和衡量工具推动成果。（00:39:24）：在科技领域，LinkedIn的广告支出回报率比其他任何社交媒体平台高出2到5倍。LinkedIn上的受众购买力是普通网络用户的两倍，而且你将与一个尊重你所处B2B世界的合作伙伴合作。让B2B营销发挥最大潜力，下次活动即可获得100美元信用额度。只需访问LinkedIn.com/podLenny即可领取信用额度。条款和条件适用。（00:39:52）：让我们实际谈谈融资这个话题，我想花点时间探讨一下。你创办的公司总共融资了多少钱，大概数字？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So Waze raised about $50 million throughout the entire journey. We started by raising 12. That was the first investment round, and then we raised the 30, and then there was the last round that we raised actually not a lot.
turns.zh: 嗯，Waze在整个过程中共融资了约5000万美元。我们从第一轮融资1200万美元开始，然后是3000万美元，最后一轮融资的金额不多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a surprising small amount of money to raise for the outcome.
turns.zh: 相较于最终成果而言，融资金额确实少得惊人。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: In general, I would say Israeli startups are leaner than American startups, so you can raise less money.
turns.zh: 总的来说，我认为以色列创业公司比美国创业公司更精简，所以他们可以融资更少的钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's amazing.
turns.zh: 是啊，这太令人惊讶了。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: At way lower valuation, unfortunately, and end up with pretty successful results.
turns.zh: 很遗憾，估值低得多，最终却取得了相当不错的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing.
turns.zh: 真是令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Raising capital, it's a journey by itself and different from the other journeys that you need only once. Raising capital is going to happen multiple times. And if we say that building a startup is a roller coaster journey, then I will say raising capital is a roller coaster journey in the dark.
turns.zh: 融资本身就是一段漫长的旅程，与那些只需经历一次的旅程截然不同。融资将是一次又一次的历程。若说创办初创公司如同坐过山车般跌宕起伏，那么我要说，融资之路就像是在黑暗中坐过山车。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like Space Mountain.
turns.zh: 这就像太空山过山车。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yeah, sort of. And one of the reason is that this is a different ballgame and you don't know how to play at the beginning. I would say a few things about raising capital for the first time. Number one, I spoke with many investors and one of the conversations that I had that they really, really resonate with me was when I spoke with one of the leading VC in Israel and asked their partner, "How long does it take you to decide if you like the entrepreneur or not?" And he asked me, "Do you want the right answer or the real answer?" Say, "You know, I heard the right answer so many times, give me the real answer." And we were sitting in a small meeting room, so the guy is looking at me and then looking at the door and looking at me again and say, "It's before they sit down." Say, "Oh, no, no, no. Say that again, right?" (00:42:02): That's the first impression. Now we all have first impression. How long does it take you to decide if you like a candidate or not? Second, you go on a date. How long does it take you to decide if you like the date? Seconds. And then maybe there are a few more minutes that you allow yourself to either change your mind or let that first impression solidifies. Now if this is the case and you're looking to raise capital, start with the strongest point at the beginning. Whatever it is, and I don't care if this is the size of the problem. This is the faction that you have. This is the team that you have built. I don't care what it is, start with that, because by the time you'll get there, they might be already setting up their mind. Then start with the strongest point at the beginning. And by the way, finish with that as well. (00:42:53): So this is the first conclusion. The second conclusion is that I spoke with early stage investors, those that invest the first money in. So company has a story to tell. That's about it, right? No traction, nothing yet is built and so forth, and I asked him, "Why did you decide to invest in this company and this company and this company?" And I spoke with many investors, and what I heard was actually pretty consistent. I like the CEO. I like the story. That's it. I like the CEO. I like the story. Now if this is the case, then there are two immediate conclusions. The first one is that the CEO goes alone to the meeting. I need the headlight on me. I don't need any distractions. I don't need my team members. I don't need anything else in the room, just me. Because if I bring other people, then at the end of the day they might say, "Yeah, I like the team, but the CEO was not specific, right? Was not unique. Was not jumping out of the pages." So CEO goes along and tell the story. (00:44:02): The other part is that they need to tell a good story, and good story is not about facts. It's about creating emotional engagement. It's about creating the sense that the listener would like to be part of this story. And for investor, it's two things. Number one is that they want to believe that this is usable, and number two, they want to believe that you can build it and this is the story that you need to tell. Now, I would say always start with the problem, right? Because guess what? Investors are also users. If they don't think that they're going to use it, so it's relevant for them, and they don't think that they're going to use it? They will basically dismiss that. They will basically say the market is not there. (00:44:52): So these are two main things. The third thing is it's a different ball game, right? So if you have product and you tell the story to potential customers, the right order of magnitude is that about one third of the listeners will buy. So in a more mature company, their pipeline is going to be three eggs in order to sell at the end of the year one eggs. One third are going to say yes. In investors, it's 1%. Not one third, 1%. So you're going to hear a hundred times no until you hear one yes. And that a hundred times no is something that you need to understand from the beginning because that's really discouraging, right? You go and speak with investors and they tell you... I call that they open up the big book of excuses why not. But in general, they are not going to invest, right? (00:45:54): Now you look at it from the other side, a venture capital partner is likely to see between a hundred and 200 companies a year and invest in one or two. 1%. That's it. So if this is the case, then it's going to be the same case for you. One out of a hundred. If you want to increase the likelihood, learn how to tell a good story, start at the strongest point at the beginning, remember that they are users, too, so their emotional engagement is going to come through the usage, the use case, and not through how big the business is.
turns.zh:
是的，某种程度上是这样的。其中一个原因是，这完全是另一回事，你一开始根本不知道该怎么玩。我想说几点关于首次融资的建议。首先，我和许多投资者交流过，其中一次对话让我印象深刻。我和以色列一位顶尖风投合伙人交谈时，问他：“你们需要多长时间才能决定是否喜欢这位创业者？”他回答：“你想听正确答案还是真实答案？”我说：“我已经听过太多正确答案了，给我真实答案吧。”当时我们坐在一个小会议室里，他先是看着我，然后看向门，又转回来看我，说：“就是在他们坐下之前。”我说：“哦，不不不，再说一遍。”（00:42:02）：这就是第一印象。现在我们都有第一印象。你判断是否喜欢一个候选人需要多长时间？几秒钟。然后可能再给几分钟时间让你改变主意或让第一印象定型。既然如此，如果你想融资，就从最强的优势点开始。无论是什么——无论是问题的规模、你现有的资源、你组建的团队，都不重要，从最强点开始，因为等你真正见面时，他们可能已经下定决心了。然后从最强点开始，最后以最强点结束。（00:42:53）：所以这是第一个结论。第二个结论是，我和早期投资者交流过，那些第一笔投资的投资者。公司有个故事可讲，对吧？没有客户，没有产品，等等。然后我问他们：“为什么决定投资这家公司？”我和许多投资者交流过，得到的回答非常一致。我喜欢CEO。我喜欢故事。仅此而已。我喜欢CEO。我喜欢故事。既然如此，有两个直接结论。第一个是CEO单独参加会议。我需要聚光灯照在我身上。我不需要任何干扰。我不需要团队成员。我不需要房间里的任何其他人，只要我自己就行。因为如果我带其他人来，最后他们可能会说：“是的，我喜欢团队，但CEO不具体，不独特，不引人入胜。”所以CEO单独讲述故事。（00:44:02）：另一部分是他们需要讲一个好故事，好的故事不是关于事实的。而是创造情感共鸣。让听众觉得自己想成为这个故事的一部分。对投资者来说，有两点。一是他们想相信这个产品有用，二是他们想相信你能把它做出来。这就是你需要讲述的故事。现在，我想说永远从问题开始，对吧？因为猜怎么着？投资者也是用户。如果他们不认为自己会使用它，那它对他们来说就无关紧要。如果他们不认为自己会使用它？他们基本上就会否定它。他们基本上会说市场不存在。（00:44:52）：所以这两个是主要点。第三点是这完全是另一回事，对吧？所以如果你有产品，你向潜在客户讲述故事时，正确的顺序是
规模效应是指，大约三分之一的听众会购买产品。因此，在一家更成熟的公司中，他们的销售流程通常是先锁定三位潜在客户，再在年底促成一笔交易。三分之一的人会表示同意。但对于投资者而言，这个比例仅为1%——不是三分之一，而是1%。所以你可能要听上百次拒绝，才能听到一次肯定。这种一百次拒绝的挫败感是创业者必须从一开始就深刻理解的，因为这确实很令人沮丧，对吧？当你去和投资者沟通时，他们会列出一大堆拒绝的理由。但总的来说，他们不会轻易投资，对吧？（00:45:54）现在从另一角度看：风险投资合伙人每年可能会评估100到200家公司，最终只会投资一两家——也就是1%。既然如此，你的情况也会一样——一百家公司中只有一家能成功。要想提高成功概率，就要学会讲好故事。先从最有力的卖点入手，要记住投资者也是用户，他们的情感共鸣来自于产品的实际使用场景，而非企业的宏大规模。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the summary at the end. I love that you summarized your points, because I try to do that. You did my job. I love this phrase you have in your book, "The dance of 100 nos."
turns.zh: 我喜欢你结尾的总结。我喜欢你把要点总结出来，因为我也一直努力这么做。你替我完成了这项任务。我特别喜欢你书里那句话——“百次拒绝的舞蹈”。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: At the beginning you look at it and you say, "Okay, they say they decided not to invest because of X, Y, Z," right? Whatever it is, right? Google can do that in no time or the market is not big enough or the market is complex or whatever it is, and then you try to argue, and you don't know that it's useless, right? It's like you go on a date and she said no, and you try to argue, right? No, there is nothing to argue anymore, right? That's no.
turns.zh: 一开始你看完别人的陈述，可能会想：“好吧，他们说因为X、Y、Z原因决定不投资。” 对吧？无论原因是什么，对吧？谷歌能很快帮你分析市场规模不足、市场复杂度高之类的问题，然后你试图反驳，但其实已经无济于事了。就好比你去约会，人家拒绝了你，你还想据理力争，对吧？但现在已经没有什么可争辩的了，对吧？这就是“不”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I look at a lot of startups too. I do a bunch of angel investing, and yeah, if it's not going to be a fit, it's just not going to work, and I could spend all this time trying to explain it to you, but nothing's going to change. And because there's other startups out there is a big part of it, right? You just want to pick the things you can that are the best, not necessarily things that are good ideas. I really like this idea of starting with your strongest point. That's such an important tactical piece of advice. To your point, investors make decisions really quickly, and so starting with something that really catches their attention, it makes so much sense because once you feel like, "Oh, wow, maybe this is a thing," your whole brain is starting to look at it from a, oh, yeah, okay, like you have a positive bend on everything you're hearing versus like, "No, no, no, this is never going to work and everything is already biased."
turns.zh: 是啊。我也经常评估很多初创公司。我做了很多天使投资，如果不合适，那就没戏了。我可以花大量时间试图说服你，但结果都一样。市场上有其他选择才是关键，对吧？你只想挑选最适合、最优质的项目，而不一定是那些看起来不错的创意。我特别喜欢先从最强优势切入的策略。这条建议太重要了。投资者决策很快，所以用最能吸引他们注意力的点开场再合适不过。一旦他们觉得“哇，或许这事儿可行”，整个大脑就会开始积极思考，而不是带着偏见说“不行，不行，这永远行不通”。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So I would add here another very strong advice. Most people are missing the most important slide of their presentation. The most important slide of your presentation is the first slide, not the one that you think about it. The first slide. The one that says Company XYZ intro. This slide is going to be presented for the longest period of time.
turns.zh: 所以我要再补充一条重要建议。大多数人忽略了演示文稿中最重要的幻灯片。首页幻灯片才是最重要的，而不是你认为重要的那张。首页幻灯片。标题是“XYZ公司介绍”。这张幻灯片会展示最久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's a good point.
turns.zh: 哇，这观点真棒。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: The longest period of time in the presentation, this slide is going to be presented on the screen and you didn't say anything there. This is the place that you're going to put your strongest point.
turns.zh: 演示文稿中展示时间最长的幻灯片，这张会一直挂在屏幕上，而你却没在上面说任何内容。这才是你要放置最强优势的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Is there an example of someone that did that or did you do that, one of your startups? What do you put there?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个做法。你有例子吗？你自己的初创公司有这么做过吗？你放在那张幻灯片上的内容是什么？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I do that all the time.
turns.zh: 我一直这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of something you put on that slide that's such a good idea?
turns.zh: 你放在那张幻灯片上的内容有什么特别好的主意？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Maybe size of the market. Maybe description of the problem. Whatever it is, right, the strongest point is there. Now the second most important slide is the last one. Not the summary. The one that says thank you. That's the time to repeat that. So most of their presentations will end up with thank you and my email, right, and this is going to be the last slide, right? Which makes sense. You just missed the opportunity. This is going to be the second-longest displayed slide of the presentation. Maybe the first.
turns.zh: 比如市场规模。或者问题描述。无论是什么，对吧？最强的优势就放在那里。现在第二重要的是最后一张幻灯片。不是总结部分。是致谢部分。这时候再重复一遍。大多数演示文稿最后都是致谢和邮箱，对吧？这才应该是最后一张幻灯片，对吧？这才合理。你只是错过了机会。这会是演示文稿中展示时间第二长的幻灯片。可能甚至是第一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Everyone's sitting there chatting, asking you questions. That's so smart. Are there any more of these tips sitting in your head to share, because these are awesome.
turns.zh: 是啊。大家都在聊天、提问。这太聪明了。你脑子里还有更多这样的技巧可以分享吗？这些都太棒了。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I do a lot of public speaking and usually my last slide says one more story and I decide on the story based on the audience and the dialogue so far and so forth. But I have many of stories, many last stories that I would like to tell. The important part is that no one is going to cut you off the stage if you have just one more story, and so this is where you can recap everything. This is where you can do whatever you want, right? Because no one is going to tell you, "Okay, time is up."
turns.zh: 我经常做公开演讲，通常我的最后一页幻灯片会写着“再讲一个故事”，然后我会根据听众反应和已有的对话内容来选择故事。但我有很多最后的故事想分享。关键是，如果你再讲一个故事，台下没人会赶你下台，这样你就能回顾整个演讲过程，自由发挥了。毕竟没人会说“好的，时间到了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, and they're not impatient because they're like, "Okay, it's almost over. Let's just let him finish."
turns.zh: 对，他们不会不耐烦，因为他们会想：“好吧，就快结束了。就让他把故事讲完吧。”

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I love that. Speaking of stories, what's the wildest fundraising story that you've been through? Is there one that comes to mind of like, "Holy shit. I can't believe that happened," or, "I can't believe that worked out"?
turns.zh: 是啊。我喜欢这种分享故事的感觉。说到最疯狂的筹款故事，你经历过最离谱的案例是什么？有没有那种让人惊呼“天啊，这事儿真发生了”，或者“这办法居然成功了”的故事？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: One of the earlier startups that I was guiding was about, eventually rolled into gift cards, but in Israel, when you return something to the store, you don't get your money back. What you get is a gift card for that particular store, right, and obviously if you return something, then it's not necessarily that you have something to buy in the store and you ended up with having a gift card that is never being used, and so why not sell this gift card? What happened is that I heard the story of the CEO and I thought that the story is not good enough, and I told him, "Look, you have to tell a better story," and asked, "Can you give me an example?" And I said, "Yeah, just imagine that," and then there was a long story about the microwave stuff working, and I bought a new one and really long, long, long story about with the details, right? How do you make a story make believe? With details. Right? The more details people think that this is real. Right? (00:51:48): If there are no details, then this is not real. So I told him this story that was like five minutes explaining, trying to fit the microwave into the closet and it didn't fit in into the cabinet, and it didn't fit in, and I had to return it to the box and so forth and whole story. And then I spoke with an investor in Israel and I told him about this new company that I'm going to invest, and I told him the same story about this microwave, right, and he said, "This is interesting. I would like to meet the CEO." Then he met the CO and CEO told him exactly the same story about the microwave. When I tell that, this is my microwave, right?This is personal. This has happened to me. And so he told me, the investor called me up later, he said, "He told me exactly the same story." So that was really funny. (00:52:44): But at the end of the day, one of the things that makes story authentic is details, because otherwise it's not, right? If you're going to tell me, okay, this is the use case of the product and you end up with explaining a use case in three lines, this is not authentic. If you watch your real users, then what happens is that you actually, and you speak with them, then you have the audacity to tell a good story. Really, really critical. If you want to tell user story, these needs to be, real or you have to learn how to tell a story with many details.
turns.zh: 我曾指导的一家早期初创公司，最终转型做礼品卡业务。但在以色列，退货时不退钱，而是给商店专用礼品卡。显然，退货后你不一定有东西可买，最后礼品卡闲置了。那为什么不把这些卡卖掉呢？我听了创始人的故事后，觉得不够精彩，就跟他说：“你得讲个更好的故事。”然后问：“能举个例子吗？”他说：“嗯，想象一下……”然后讲了一大堆微波炉的故事，买新微波炉，各种细节，太冗长了。要让故事可信，就得有细节，对吧？如果没有细节，就不真实。所以我给他讲了这个故事，五分钟讲微波炉的故事，试图把它塞进橱柜，结果塞不进，最后退货等等。然后我跟以色列的一位投资者聊起这家新公司，跟他讲了微波炉的故事，他说：“这很有意思，我想见见创始人。”结果创始人给他讲了一模一样的微波炉故事。我说：“这是我的微波炉啊。”太私人了。这事儿真的发生在我身上。后来投资者打电话给我说：“他讲的故事跟你一模一样。”太搞笑了。（00:51:48）但说到底，细节是故事真实性的关键，否则就假了。如果你只讲产品用例，三句话就完了，那不真实。要观察真实用户，跟他们交流，然后你才能讲出精彩的故事。这点至关重要。如果你想讲用户故事，必须真实，或者学会如何用细节讲述。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But interestingly, it sounds like the story itself doesn't have to have happened to you in real life. It could be a made-up story, but with a lot of details is the lesson there. Interesting.
turns.zh: 但有趣的是，这个故事本身似乎不必发生在你现实生活中。它可能是虚构的，但其中包含诸多细节，这才是关键所在。真有意思。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep. If you tell it very briefly, then it doesn't sound right.
turns.zh: 是啊。如果你把它讲得太简略，听起来就不太对劲了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Any other advice along those lines? I want to talk about two more chapters before we wrap up. Is there anything else around fundraising that you think is important for people to know?
turns.zh: 太棒了。还有其他相关建议吗？在结束之前，我想再讨论两章内容。关于筹款方面，你觉得还有哪些信息对大家很重要？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So I will tell you which chapters I would like to speak about.
turns.zh: 那我来告诉你我打算讲哪两章内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. I wonder what they are. I wonder if they're the same.
turns.zh: 好啊。我很好奇它们是什么内容。不知道是不是一样的。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Understanding users and firing and hiring.
turns.zh: 用户理解、解雇与招聘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, firing and hiring. That was on my list. Okay. Let's start there and then understanding users wasn't, but I'm excited to hear what you have to say there.
turns.zh: 好的，解雇与招聘。这在我的清单上呢。好的，我们就从这部分开始吧。用户理解部分倒不在清单上，不过我很期待听听你对此的见解。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So I send the book proposal to many publisher, and there is one chapter that says firing and hiring, and many of them came back and say, "Oh, it should be hiring and firing." And I said, "No. Firing is hard decision. Hiring is easy decisions." You have to first of all learn how to make the hard decisions. Now, the inspirations for this chapter came from many dialogues that I had with entrepreneurs that their startup failed, and I asked them, "Why, what happened?" And about half told me the team was not right, and I kept on asking, "Okay, what do you mean the team was not right?" And what I heard the most is, "We had this guy not good enough and this guy not good enough." So this is what I heard the most. (00:54:58): Another thing that I heard quite often is that we had communication issues, right? Something that I actually called ego management issues. And then asked them the most interesting question, "When did you know that the team is not right?" Now the answer was actually rather scary. All of them told me within the first month. Then you said, "Wait a minute. If you knew within the first month that the team is not right and you didn't do anything, the problem was not that the team was not right. The problem was that the CEO did not make hard decision." Making hard decisions is hard. Making easy decisions. This is why no one likes to make the hard decisions, because you need to live with the consequences. In a small place like a startup, the hard decisions will always go to the top. Now, if the CEO does not make that hard decisions, the result is always the same. The top performing people would leave. Now, they would leave because they don't want to be in a place that is unable to make hard decisions and they have a choice. (00:56:02): The nature of the beast is different. Startup is a small organization. Just imagine that you are a small organization, like could be a team, whatever it is, right? 10, 20, 30 people, and there is someone that shouldn't be there, and I don't care if that someone shouldn't be there because they are way underperforming or because they are assholes. I don't really care. They shouldn't be there. Everyone knows. Everyone knows and the CEO doesn't do anything. That's the nature of the beast and this is why top performing people would leave. Now, building a startup is really, really hard, right? It's hard if you have the right team, but if you have people that shouldn't be there that are still there and the top performing people are leaving, then it's going to be mission impossible. The conclusion of this chapter is really, really interesting. If everyone knows within a month and every time that you hire someone new, what I really want you to do is mark your calendars for 30 days down the road and ask yourself one question, "Knowing what I know today, would I hire this person?" (00:57:16): At the end of the day, I'd like to nail that into yes or no, right? Because this is where decisions are being made easily. If you ask yourself that question, if the answer is yes, then go to this person and tell them that you are really excited that they've joined, they are exceeding your expectations, and give them more equity, and you buy their loyalty for life. If the answer is no, fire them immediately. They're already set on a trajectory of not being successful and they're creating damage to you, to the rest of the team and to themselves, right? They deserve to be successful, but it's not going to happen here. They deserve to find someplace else that they can be successful, but it's not going to happen here, and that decision is really, really dramatic. (00:58:08): Now, in many cases with hard decisions, we know what is the right decisions. We are looking for confirmation. If you look for confirmation, then go and speak with the top performing people and tell them, ask them the following, right? "Assuming XYZ person is going to leave, how sore are you going to feel?" And you will be surprised that they are going to tell you, "Oh, it's not a big deal." This is your confirmation.
turns.zh:
于是我把这本书的提案发送给许多出版商，其中有一章讲解“解雇与招聘”问题。很多出版商回复说：“哦，应该改成‘招聘与解雇’。”我回应道：“不行。解雇是艰难的决定，招聘反而是容易的决定。”你首先得学会如何做出艰难的抉择。写这章的灵感来自于我与许多创业者的对话——他们的初创公司失败后，我问他们：“为什么？发生了什么？” 大约一半的人告诉我，“团队不合适”。我追问：“团队哪里不合适？” 最常听到的回答是：“这个人不行，那个人也不行。”这就是最常见的借口。

（00:54:58）另一个常见问题是沟通不畅，我称之为“自我管理问题”。最有意思的追问是：“你什么时候意识到团队不合适？” 他们的回答令人震惊——几乎都是在入职第一个月就发现问题。但关键问题是：如果入职首月就察觉团队不行却无所作为，那根本不是团队的问题，而是CEO未能果断决策的结果。做出艰难决定太难了，但做出简单决定却容易。这就是人们不愿面对挑战的原因——你必须承担后果。在初创公司这样的小型组织里，艰难决策必然由高层承担。CEO若不果断，优秀人才必将离场。

（00:56:02）初创公司的本质不同。小型组织（如团队）中，若有不称职的人存在——无论是业绩低下还是品行恶劣——大家心知肚明却无人作为。这就是人才流失的根源。构建初创公司极其困难：有优秀团队固然美好，但当不称职者长期占据位置而优秀者不断离去时，任务就变得不可能完成。

本章的核心结论是：如果团队在入职首月就暴露问题，你需要每隔30天回顾并自问：“以今天的认知，我还会招聘这个人吗？” （00:57:16）最终判断必须明确：是或否。这才是果断决策的关键。若答案是肯定的，就热情接纳并赋予更多股权；若否，则立即解雇。他们注定难成大器，只会拖累团队和自身。成功的机会在别处，但绝非此处。
那个决定真是太令人震惊了。（00:58:08）：在许多需要做出艰难抉择的情况下，我们明明知道正确的决策是什么，但却总在寻求确认。如果你想获得确认，那就去找表现最出色的员工，问他们这个问题："假设XYZ要离开了，你会有多难过？" 你会惊讶地发现，他们会告诉你："哦，这没什么大不了的。" 这就是你所需要的确认。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. We had Elizabeth Stone from Netflix, the CTO of Netflix on, and she talked about this thing they called a keeper test, which is exactly that, where every manager is always asking themselves, "If this person were to leave tomorrow and tell me they're leaving, would I fight to keep them? And if not, I should just, I need to let them go," and that's always top of mind for managers there.
turns.zh: 是的。我们邀请了Netflix的首席技术官伊丽莎白·斯通（Elizabeth Stone）来分享，她谈到了他们所谓的“留才测试”。这个测试的核心就是，每位管理者都要时刻自问：“如果这个人明天要离职，并且告诉我他要走了，我会竭尽全力挽留他吗？如果不会，那就应该放手让他走。”这始终是Netflix管理层最关注的问题。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: You know, one of my companies had a pretty good year and they decided to have an annual bonuses by and large to nearly all of the employees. And then I asked the CEO, "So how did you end up with the list?" And he said, "Okay. We had these people that getting twice as much the others, and then the others, and then there are four people that are not going to get anything." And I asked them, "Are they still here?" They shouldn't be here, right? If they are so much underperforming, then they shouldn't be here. But generally you need the time to ask yourself the tough questions because only then you can answer them, right? If you don't ask the tough questions, then you don't answer them.
turns.zh: 你知道吗，我所在的一家公司去年业绩不错，他们决定给几乎所有员工发放年度奖金。然后我问CEO：“那你们怎么确定名单？”他说：“嗯，我们把那些表现超出其他人两倍的人列出来，再把其他人分成两组，最后还有四个人拿不到奖金。”我问：“他们现在还在公司吗？”他们不应该在啊，对吧？如果表现这么差，就不该留。可通常你需要时间问自己这些难题，因为只有这样才能找到答案。如果不问难题，就永远得不到答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I really love this very tactical piece of advice, which I was definitely going to touch on, of putting a calendar entry into your calendar when you hire someone 30 days in to remind yourself, asking yourself, "Would I hire this person knowing what I know now? And if not, you should probably let them go."
turns.zh: 是啊。我特别喜欢这个非常务实的建议——我肯定会提到的，就是在招聘新员工30天后，就在日历上设置提醒，问自己：“如果现在知道这些信息，我还会雇用这个人吗？如果不会，那就该放他走了。”

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: By the way, I can tell you that for everything in your life, right? Everything in your life, ask yourself, "Knowing what you know today, would you do something different?"
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我觉得这适用于你生活中的每一件事，对吧？每一件事。问自己：“以现在所知的信息，你会做出不同的选择吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: If the answer is yes, then do something different today. Today is the first day of the rest of your life.
turns.zh: 如果答案是肯定的，那就从今天开始行动。今天就是你余生第一天。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is powerful advice. So what I'm thinking there is if I bought something, maybe return it. What else have you applied that to in your life?
turns.zh: 这真是个强有力的建议。所以我在想，如果我买了什么东西，或许该退货。还有哪些方面你用过这个方法？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Relationship in general. Directions that you're going, right? Do you still like that? I have five children and they're all in their twenties and beginning of thirties and they struggle with their career path, and I basically tell them, "Look, if you are going to work in a place and you don't like it, then what I want you to do is ask yourself why you are not liking it and whether or not there is something that you can change, and I'm going to ask you the same question in 90 days from now, and if this still is the case, then quit."
turns.zh: 比如人际关系。人生方向，对吧？你还喜欢现在走的路吗？我有五个孩子，他们都二十多岁或三十出头，在职业发展上遇到了瓶颈。我基本上会告诉他们：“听着，如果你不喜欢现在的工作环境，那就问问自己为什么不喜欢，有没有可以改变的地方。90天后我再问你同样的问题，如果还是这样，那就辞职。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interestingly you make that 90 days, which it kind of applies some decisions. You need to wait a little bit more. You need more data. You need more time than necessarily 30 days, but set some kind of timeline.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，你把时间定为90天，这似乎适用于很多决定。你需要多等一阵子。你需要更多数据。30天可能不够，但总得设个时间节点。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: If you don't set a timeline, it'll never happen.
turns.zh: 如果不设时间节点，事情永远不会推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the other really interesting implication here is most decisions are a two-way door. Most decisions, you can change your mind. You can quit. You can leave a relationship. I was thinking you were going to say with your five kids 30 days after they're born, "Do I still want this kid 30 days with knowing what I know now?" I'm glad you didn't go there.
turns.zh: 我觉得另一个很有意思的启示是，大多数决定都是双向选择。大多数决定都可以改变主意。你可以辞职。你可以结束一段关系。我原本以为你会说，在孩子出生30天后问：“知道现在所知信息，我还想要这个孩子吗？” 还好你没这么说。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: No, this is different, right? You go into this journey of having children with the understanding that this is long journey. Go into this journey of building a startup with the understanding that this is a long journey, right? The fact that it's going to be hard? Okay, so it's hard. It is hard, by the way. But yeah, the decisions that obviously they need to be relative to their duration, right? So yeah, raising kids is a long journey.
turns.zh: 嗯，这不一样，对吧？生孩子这件事，本来就知道这是一段漫长的旅程。创业同样如此，对吧？困难是必然的。没错，创业之路确实艰难。但关键是，决策必须与时长相匹配，对吧？所以养育孩子确实是一段漫长的旅程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a one-way door, also. Is there anything else you wanted to say around the hiring and firing concept? Clearly firing is the main lesson here, is get really good at firing, firing quickly and decisively.
turns.zh: 这也是条单行道。关于招聘与解雇的概念，你还有什么想说的吗？显然，解雇才是关键教训——要学会高效、果断地解雇员工。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: You know, there are tons of advices in the book and eventually I will tell, even in the hiring process, right, most of us are going to interview candidates and then decide that they like or dislike the candidate, but they don't know. Then speak with someone that does know. Speak with the reference.
turns.zh: 书中有很多建议。最后我会分享一些，尤其是在招聘过程中，我们大多会面试候选人，然后根据喜好或厌恶做决定，但其实这些判断往往不准确。这时就需要去找真正了解他们的人——比如推荐人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite question you like to ask references? Is there something that you find is really helpful to tell you? Give you honest insight?
turns.zh: 你有没有最喜欢的询问推荐人的问题？有没有特别有用的见解能帮助你？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: For reference?
turns.zh: 对于推荐人？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: That's really simple. Would you hire him? Or would you hire her, right? So essentially at the end of the day you want to nail it into yes or no.
turns.zh: 其实很简单。会雇用他吗？或者她？归根结底，你要给出明确的答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And hope that they're being honest. That's sometimes a challenge.
turns.zh: 是的。关键是希望对方诚实。这有时是个挑战。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: No, if they will tell me yes, then I would ask them, "Why didn't you?" Someone asked me for a reference on someone that I really enjoyed working with. I really think highly of them, and he asked me if they can schedule a call for half an hour and I said, "Look, I'm traveling. I don't really have time. But if you want an email in one word, take the guy." And then he was trying to outsmart and ask me back, "Can I have that in two words?" And I said, "Yeah, take the guy fast." When you know, you know. That's it.
turns.zh: 不，如果对方说会雇用，那我会反问：“你为什么没雇用？”有人让我给一个我很欣赏的同事写推荐信。我对他评价很高，但他只想约半小时通话，我说：“我正在出差，实在没时间。但如果你需要一句话评价，那就雇用他吧。”结果他想耍点小聪明反问：“能用两句话评价吗？”我回答：“快雇用他。”当你心知肚明时，就知道该怎么做了。就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. That's what you want to be looking for. Okay. Amazing. So let's do one more chapter. The one I was going to pick, you choose what you're more excited about, is selling a company. Your last chapter exit. The one you were thinking about going to is talking to users. I imagine that's much more applicable to more people, so that's probably the better choice, but your choice.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种思路。这才是你该关注的重点。好极了。那我们再看最后一章。我本来想选卖公司这部分，但你更感兴趣的是用户访谈。我觉得后者对更多人更有实用价值，所以还是选用户访谈吧，不过还是听你的。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Okay, then let's stick with understanding users. Steve Wozniak, co-founder of Apple, wrote the foreword to my book and he called it the Bible for entrepreneurs, and when I sent him the first chapter, he said, "Wow, I wish I had that When I started." I met Steve Wozniak for the first time about 10 years ago. We spoke at the same conference in Guatemala, and look, when I grew up, Steve Wozniak was my technological guru, right so he was the most important person in the technology space in my mind. And then we spoke at the same conference and we had dinner the night before, and the only thing that actually was really important for me is to have a selfie with my idol, right? And so I took up my iPhone and with the iPhone you can take pictures by clicking here on the screen or using the volume button on the side, right? (01:05:34): And so I took a selfie with him holding the phone like that and clicking on the volume button and he said, "Finally." And I said, "Finally what?" "Finally someone using it the way that I meant it to be." Now you realize that there is no right or wrong. There are different people that are using different products in different ways, and occasionally if I would have large audience, then I would ask the people, "Okay, how do you use Waze?" Right? "So you go to your destination and you enter destination, and then Waze guides you through the screen with the display of the maneuvers that needs to be made or with the audio guidance of turn right, turn left and so forth. If you are watching the screen, raise your hand." And then I would have about 70% of the people raise their hand." Then I ask people to watch around them and see those people. Then I ask, "If you are listening to the audio prompt, raise your hand." Then I have about 20 or 30 more percent of the people raising their hand. And again, I send people to watch around and see those hands. (01:06:41): There is no right or wrong. Different people are using it differently. Now, if you are using Waze in a certain way, up until this moment, you didn't know that there are other people that are using it differently, and to be frank, you don't care. You getting your own value the way that you get it, then you don't really care that there are other people that are getting it differently. But if you are building a product and you don't know that, then you are building the wrong product. You don't know that there are other people that are not like you, and you think that you're building the product for yourself, then you're making a big mistake. And the way to figure it out is, by the way, two things. Number one, watch new users. Simply watch users and see what they're doing. And number two, if they're not doing what you expect them to do, then ask them why, because this why is the one that is going to make your product successful. You understand the why and the next version you're going to address that. (01:07:42): Now, this is in particular when it comes to understanding users. Obviously there are a lot of users, but we can group them into several groups of their ability to adapt something new, and something new is not necessarily new technology. We think about it as a new technology, but it's not necessarily about technology. It's about new behavior, right? And then we look at the entire population and every time that we look into large numbers, they will have normal distribution, right? So the bell curve of the distribution, and then we will have about 2% of the populations that they're the innovatives. The innovatives are going to use something new because it's new. That's it. They care about this subject and they going to be the first one to hear about it and they're going to try that out because it's new. The second group is usually what we will get to see as the first users are the early adapters. As soon as they realize that there is value, they're going to give it a try. And if there is value, then they will keep on using it, and if there is no value, then they will quit. Right? (01:08:55): The third group is the most important group. This is where market leaders are, right? This is called the early majority. This is about one third of the population, and the one that wins the early majority wins the market. The challenge with this group, with the people in this group, is that they're afraid of change. So their state of mind is, don't rock the boat. Whatever I'm currently doing is good enough for me. So if you have Salesforce.com, which is absolutely amazing, their reaction is going to be, "What's wrong with Excel?" And because they're afraid of change, they are not going to try something new.
