Now the reason is that at the end of the day, they're afraid that this is going to be too complex for them and they will not get it, and they don't want to be embarrassed and they don't want to feel like idiots. And guess what? People don't like to feel like idiots, and so they are not going to try. And you need to see those people to understand their barriers for starting to use your service. (01:10:02): And by the way, the solution is always the same. Simplicity. Leonardo da Vinci said that simplicity is the ultimate sophistication. If you want to make it simple, in your journey of building a product, we basically say this is iteration to iteration to iteration. In many of those you add features and you add features and you add features until you all of a sudden you add the features that people are using. What you really want to do next is remove the rest of the features that people are not using because they're adding complexity. Now, most of the product owners, they're either innovators or early adopters. You cannot understand an early majority person. If you belong to one group, you cannot understand a person from that group unless you watch them and [inaudible 01:10:57]. So the most important part of understanding users is actually seeing those users. And they are not wrong. This is how they behave.
turns.zh:
好的，那我们继续来谈用户理解。苹果公司的联合创始人史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克为我的书写了序言，他称其为"创业者的圣经"。当我把第一章发给他时，他说："哇，我真希望自己创业时能有这本书。"大约十年前，我第一次见到史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克。我们在危地马拉的同一场会议上发言。回想起来，在我成长过程中，史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克就是我的科技偶像，对我来说，他是科技领域最重要的人物。我们在同一场会议上发言，前一天晚上共进晚餐。对我来说，最重要的事就是和偶像合张自拍，对吧？于是我拿出 iPhone，按下屏幕上的快门键，或者用侧边的音量键拍摄照片。（01:05:34）我用这种方式拍了张自拍照，沃兹尼亚克说"终于等到了。"我问"终于等到什么？"他回答"终于有人用正确的方式操作了。"现在你会意识到，没有所谓的正确或错误。不同的人会以不同的方式使用同一款产品。有时如果听众规模较大，我会问："好的，你们怎么用 Waze 导航？"对吧？"你输入目的地后，Waze 会通过屏幕上的导航指示或语音提示引导你转弯。举手示意正在看屏幕的人。"然后约70%的人举手。接着我让他们环顾四周，看看周围的人也在这么做。再问："如果你们听从语音提示操作，举手吧。"又有20%到30%的人举手。我再次让他们观察周围的人举手。（01:06:41）没有对错之分。不同的人使用方式不同。如果你目前的 Waze 使用方式是正确的，那你可能并不知道还有其他人用法不同，说实话，你也不在乎。你用自己的方式获取价值，就无需在意其他人用法不同。但如果你开发产品却不了解这一点，那你就选错了方向。你以为自己在为自己开发产品，却忽略了其他人的需求。这时候有两个关键点：第一，观察新用户。简单地观察用户行为。第二，如果他们的行为不符合预期，就询问原因，因为这些原因正是产品成功的关键。理解了原因，下一版本就能针对性改进。
就是这样。他们关心这个主题，会率先知晓相关消息，并因其新奇性而尝试使用。第二类人群通常是我们最先接触到的——早期采用者。一旦他们意识到其价值，就会付诸实践。若确有价值，他们会持续使用；若无价值，便会放弃。对吧？（01:08:55）第三类人群最为关键。这里是市场领导者的阵营，称作早期多数派，约占总人口的三分之一。一旦赢得早期多数派的支持，就能占领市场。但这个群体面临挑战——他们惧怕变革，秉持“别打破现状”的心态。他们会说：“Excel不好用吗？” 正因恐惧变革，他们不愿尝试新事物。归根结底，他们担心复杂性超出承受范围，担心难堪或显得愚蠢。猜猜怎么着？人们不愿被视为傻瓜，所以宁可按兵不动。要理解他们的使用障碍，就必须观察这些群体。（01:10:02）解决之道始终如一——简化。达芬奇曾说：“大道至简。” 在产品迭代过程中，我们秉持“不断迭代、不断迭代、再迭代”的理念。不断添加功能，直至用户真正需要的功能浮出水面。接下来，要去除冗余功能，避免增加复杂性。多数产品经理要么是创新者，要么是早期采用者。若不深入观察早期多数派，你永远无法理解他们的行为模式。理解用户最关键的环节在于观察他们的真实行为。他们的选择无可厚非，这就是他们的行为逻辑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a couple of threads there I'll pull out. One is look for surprising uses of your product because, as you said, you'll realize, "Oh, some people are using this in a way that I didn't expect," and it'll remind you people are not the way you are and don't assume that they're going to want exactly what you're building, so pay attention to things that surprise you. We had Jeffrey Moore on the podcast and he talked through a lot of this stuff, and one of the lessons there to help you bridge that gap from, to the, what is it, the third group? How did you describe it? The late majority?
turns.zh: 接下来，我要提几个要点。在这里，我会重点讲讲如何发现产品意外的使用场景。正如你所说，当你意识到"有些人用产品的用法完全出乎你的意料"时，这会提醒你，用户的需求和你的设想并不一致，不要想当然地认为他们一定会喜欢你所开发的产品。所以，要留意那些让你感到惊讶的细节。我们在播客中邀请了杰弗里·摩尔（Jeffrey Moore），他详细讲解了这些内容。其中一个关键点是，如何缩小与用户的认知鸿沟？你提到的第三个群体是什么？你怎么描述的？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: The early majority.
turns.zh: 早期多数派。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The early majority.
turns.zh: 早期多数派。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Late majority will never use the product. They will use your product only if they have to.
turns.zh: 晚期多数派永远不会使用你的产品。除非迫不得已，他们才会用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The laggards, I think he calls it. They look for basically references. People telling them, "Hey, you really need to use this." A lot of people, just like basically word-of-mouth is the way you described it.
turns.zh: 对。滞后者，我记得他是这么称呼他们的。他们基本上是在寻找参考案例。有人会告诉他们："嘿，你真的需要用这个。"很多人，正如你所描述的，靠口口相传就能传播。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: No, not just word-of-mouth. Even occasionally someone to show them how to use it.
turns.zh: 不，不只是口口相传。有时甚至会有人亲自教他们如何使用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That makes sense. Just like, "Here, check out Waze. Here's how it works." Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Okay. Amazing. Is there anything else along those lines as you're talking to customers and understanding what you're looking for that you want to share?
turns.zh: 对。这很合理。比如："来，看看Waze。它是这样用的。"对，这很有道理。好的，太棒了。还有其他类似的见解吗？在与客户交流、了解他们的需求时，你有没有想分享的经验？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Occasionally what happens is that we speak with the wrong customers. So just imagine that we have what I call funnel of use, right? So on top of the funnel, we have people that are download the app, let's say, or have entered their website, and then the next phase is that they registered and the next phase that they're trying to use it for the first time and then the next phase is that they're getting the value and they're coming back, right? In this funnel, what we usually try to do is speak with the users at the bottom of the funnels, those that were successful. But in order to improve, we need to speak with those that fail, those that were unsuccessful, those that did not register, or they did register and did not use, or they did use and did not come back, because they know something that we really need to know. Why? This why is what makes a great product.
turns.zh: 有时候我们会和错误的客户交流。想象一下我们有一个用户使用漏斗，对吧？漏斗顶端是下载应用或访问网站的人。接下来是注册阶段，再到首次使用阶段，最后是获得价值并回访阶段。在这个漏斗中，我们通常会和成功用户交流，但要改进产品，就需要和失败者对话——那些未注册、注册后未使用、使用后未回访的人，因为他们知道我们急需了解的关键信息。为什么？这就是打造伟大产品的秘诀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I imagine you could also fall into danger there if people that just aren't a fit for your product, there's just no point wasting your time on people that are just not going to be a fit. So is the idea there find people that are really far down the funnel but still bounced and churned?
turns.zh: 有意思。我想如果你遇到不适合产品的人，就没必要在他们身上浪费时间了。所以关键是找到那些在漏斗底部但又流失掉的用户？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Amazing. Okay. So we've gone through all the chapters I was hoping to go through, plus the ones you were excited about. Final thing before we get to our very exciting lightning round, we have a segment on this podcast called Fail Corner, where I ask a guest to share a time they failed in their career and what they learned from that experience, and I'm curious if there is a story that comes to mind of a time that you failed either in a startup or as you were an employee somewhere and how that was important to you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们已经讨论完了希望探讨的所有章节，以及你感兴趣的内容。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，我们播客有一个名为“失败角落”的环节，我会邀请嘉宾分享他们职业生涯中的失败经历以及从中吸取的教训。我很好奇你是否能想到在创业公司或作为员工时失败的经历，以及这对你的重要性。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So number one, I reserve the right for my biggest failure yet to come. And look, I keep on trying new things. I keep on doing things, and so eventually I will fail as much as... Maybe I'm more successful statistically than others, but I will fail, and this is very, very important part to realize. Don't be afraid to fail, right? In your journey, you're going to fail multiple times, and when you fail and get up, you get up stronger. This is maybe something that I will tell all the parents in the world. The biggest advice that I can give you is teach your children to fail. Because when they get up, they get up stronger, and when they know that they will get out of their comfort zone and they will eventually discover what makes them happy. At the end of the day, as parents, there's only one thing that we really like. We want our kids to be happy in their own way. We don't know what it is. They don't know what it is. We want them to explore, and they will only explore if they are not afraid to fail.
turns.zh: 好的。首先，我要保留自己至今最大失败的权利。看吧，我一直在尝试新事物，不断行动，最终我肯定会失败无数次……或许从数据上看，我比别人更成功，但失败终将降临，而认识到这一点至关重要。别害怕失败，对吧？在人生旅途中，你会多次遭遇挫折，但每次跌倒后重新站起，你就会变得更强大。或许我会把这句话送给全天下的父母。我能给出的最重要建议，就是教会孩子们勇于失败。因为当他们站起来时，会变得更坚韧，当他们敢于走出舒适区，最终就能找到属于自己的快乐源泉。说到底，作为父母，我们唯一的愿望就是让孩子以自己的方式获得幸福。我们不知道他们要什么，他们自己也不确定。但我们希望他们去探索，而探索的前提就是不惧怕失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This is a very timely advice for me because our kid is always falling down and it's always this balance between helping them not fall and letting them figure things out.
turns.zh: 是啊。这对我来说真是及时雨，因为我们家孩子老是摔倒，总要在扶一把和放手让他们自己探索之间权衡。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Let them fall. There is a Japanese saying, fall seven times and get up eight.
turns.zh: 就让他们摔吧。有句话叫七次跌倒，八次爬起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Uri, is there anything else that you wanted to share or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 乌里，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享或留给他们的吗？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: No, I think that was actually, I really enjoyed it.
turns.zh: 没有了。我觉得今天真的很愉快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well, we're not done yet. We've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们还没结束呢，马上就要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. First question, what are two or three books that you recommended most to other people other than your own book?
turns.zh: 好的。第一个问题，除了你自己的书，你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Mark Randolph of Netflix. That Will Never Work, right? And by the way, it's funny. Mark Randolph wrote endorsement to my book and I reached out to him because I read someplace that he's answering all of his emails, and I reached, I sent him an email and said, "Look, we have at least three things in common. Number one, I do answer all of my emails as well. Number two, I'm using your product, you are using mine. And number three, I heard more time that will never work than you did." And I think that understanding this journey is really, really important, so this is definitely a book that I would recommend. Atomic Habits. Getting habits and improving them, measuring and improving, is really, really important.
turns.zh: Netflix的马克·兰道夫（Mark Randolph）吧。《这永远行不通》（That Will Never Work），对吧？顺便说一句，这本书很有趣。马克·兰道夫给我写了推荐信，我联系他是因为我在某处看到他会回复所有邮件，我就给他发邮件说：“看，我们至少有三点共同点。第一，我也会回复所有邮件。第二，我们都在使用对方的产品。第三，我听过《这永远行不通》比你听得还多。”我觉得理解这个过程真的非常非常重要，所以这本书我绝对会推荐。还有《原子习惯》（Atomic Habits）。养成并改进习惯，衡量和优化，真的非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool choices. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 很棒的选择。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I don't watch a lot.
turns.zh: 我不怎么看电视。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Easy, then. Do you have a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 那简单了。你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: So I can bet that most of the people say the ChatGPT, but actually no. I recently downloaded the Chess App and I returned to play chess with the computer or something that I haven't done for so many years, and I really enjoy that.
turns.zh: 我敢打赌大多数人都会说ChatGPT，但其实不是。我最近下载了国际象棋应用，又开始和电脑下棋了，这是我多年没做过的事，我真的很享受这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. It's actually, I don't think ChatGPT has ever been recommended. Recent choices have been a beautiful Persian rug, a Rivian, a very nice Mercedes, and I think recently it was a course on nervous system regulation.
turns.zh: 太棒了。实际上，我觉得ChatGPT从未被推荐过。最近推荐的有漂亮的波斯地毯、Rivian电动车、豪华奔驰车，还有最近推荐的神经系统调节课程。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All over the place. Two final questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find really useful in work, your own life? It may be the one on your shirt, but is there any other that you come back to often and find useful?
turns.zh: 真是五花八门。最后两个问题：你有没有最喜欢的的人生格言，在工作和生活中觉得特别实用？可能就是你衬衫上的那句，但有没有其他你经常回味并觉得有用的？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: Don't be afraid to fail. I think that in many cases we need to accept the fact that we don't know.
turns.zh: 别怕失败。我觉得在很多情况下，我们需要接受自己无知的事实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Important words. Final question, is there a problem you're starting to fall in love with more recently, maybe tinkering with a new startup idea? Or are you done with starting companies?
turns.zh: 重要的话题。最后一个问题，你最近有没有开始热衷于某个问题？比如构思新创业项目？还是说你已经厌倦了创业？

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: I probably will never be done. I have 10 different startups in multiple areas. One of them, Pontera helps people to retire richer, which is one of the biggest challenges in the world in general, but also in the U.S. If I would ask a hundred people on the street that have 401k plans, "What is your 401k plan invested at?" 95% of them will tell me, "I don't know." I do know, by the way. In the default. Whatever was the default when they joined, right? Now obviously if you didn't do anything and you think it's right, no, it's not right. It's probably simply not enough. So this is a big problem. I have one in the medical space that is trying to create, I would call that the AI of the medical knowledge, so trying to improve doctors, and in particular in clinical decisions. That is going to change the world. (01:19:27): But if you would ask me, then I will give you some examples, right? So mobility is still a problem, right? You look at many areas in our lifetime and mobility is still, every year it's, instead of getting better, it's getting lesser. So mobility is still a problem. And medical services, right? U.S. medical services are five to 10 times more expensive than they are in Germany. Now, it's not that they're better. They're simply more expensive. So obviously you ask yourself, "Okay, where is this inefficiency? Where is it?" Right? A lot of places of inefficiency in the medical services if they're so expensive. Education. Okay. Anything that I will tell you that we are still doing the same way that our parents did is probably something that we need to revisit.
turns.zh: 我可能永远不会停止。我在多个领域有10个不同的创业项目。其中一个叫Pontera，帮助人们退休后更富有。这是全球乃至美国最大的挑战之一。如果我问100个有401(k)计划的人：“你的401(k)投资在哪里？”95%的人会说：“我不知道。”其实我知道，默认设置就是加入时选择的那个，对吧？但显然如果你什么都不做，还觉得没问题，那就大错特错了。很可能根本不够。所以这是个大问题。我在医疗领域的项目，致力于打造医疗知识的人工智能，帮助医生提升水平，尤其是在临床决策方面。这将改变世界。（01:19:27）但如果你想听具体例子，我可以举几个。对吧？交通问题依然存在，对吧？看看我们生活中的很多领域，交通问题依然存在。每年情况非但没有改善，反而越来越糟。所以交通问题依然是个难题。医疗服务方面，美国的医疗服务费用是德国的五到十倍。问题不在于它们更好，仅仅是更贵。所以你不禁会问：“效率低下在哪里？在哪里？” 对吧？医疗服务存在诸多低效率的地方，既然如此贵。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I nerd sniped you with falling in love with problems. Clearly fall in love with a lot of problems. You want to solve them all. You're addicted to startups.
turns.zh: 我感觉我用对问题的痴迷来抢了你的风头。显然我痴迷于很多问题。你想解决所有问题。你对创业上瘾了。

turns.speaker: Uri Levine
turns.en: The good news is that there are a lot of problems and the bad news that there are lots of problems.
turns.zh: 好消息是问题很多，坏消息是问题太多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're there to solve it. I love it. Uri, your book is amazing. It's incredibly practical, full of tons of advice that every founder should read, and it goes from idea all the way to exit. So basically, no matter where you're on the journey, the book is going to be useful to you. Tell people where to find it and where they can follow you for more stuff that you share over time, and then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 而你就是来解决这些问题的。我喜欢这样。乌里，你的书太棒了。内容极其实用，满载每个创始人都应该阅读的建议，从创意到退出全流程覆盖。所以无论你处于创业旅程的哪个阶段，这本书都会对你有用。告诉听众在哪里能找到它，以及他们可以关注你获取更多分享内容的方式。然后听众如何能对你有所帮助？
